name: Fulvic acid supplement

lead: Fulvic acid is the fraction of humic substances, formed as organic matter decomposes over long periods, that dissolves at any pH. Supplement makers sell it as mineral drops, powders and capsules, often derived from shilajit, a tar-like substance from Himalayan and other mountain rock.

Users take it hoping for more energy and recovery, which they connect to training and looking healthier. Reviews describe antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and adaptogenic findings from lab, animal and some human work on shilajit, and say well-controlled studies of standardised products are still needed.

paras: It is taken orally as a liquid, powder or capsule, sometimes inside multi-ingredient stacks that pair a shilajit fulvic complex with ingredients such as CoQ10 and PQQ. Strength and composition vary across products.

Raw or poorly purified shilajit has been found to contain hazardous heavy metals including lead, so purity matters. Fulvic acid can also bind metals, and variability of composition has been highlighted as a research limitation.

social.title: Fulvic acid and 84 essential minerals for optimal performance and Health

chain: Claimed antioxidant effects and reduced fatigue
More training capacity and recovery, supporting physique and skin health (claimed)
angle.text: Users take it for energy and recovery, hoping for better training output and general health that shows in the physique. These links are claimed rather than established in trials of fulvic acid itself.

lead: Fulvic acid is the humic-substance fraction soluble at any pH, formed by long decomposition of biomass and found in soil, peat, coal and water. [1][2] Shilajit, the mountain exudate used in Ayurvedic, Chinese and Tibetan traditions, is roughly 60-80% humic substances including humic and fulvic acids. [3]

In supplement form it is sold as a mineral or vitality aid. Lifting-forum users have mentioned it for recovery and as an ingredient in stacks, and a 2014 review reported that shilajit is used as a revitaliser, with animal and human data indicating improved physical performance and reduced fatigue. [4][4][5]

Researchers say rigorous human trials on standardised products are lacking. A 2025 review of humic substances describes antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in lab work and notes composition variability. [6] A Wikipedia summary states that antioxidant and immunomodulatory claims lack scientific validation and cites a 2024 systematic review suggesting a purified extract may raise testosterone in men with late-onset hypogonadism. [3]

paras: Humic substances comprise humic acid, fulvic acid and humin; the concept dates to Franz Achard's alkaline extraction in 1786, and Berzelius isolated aquatic humic substances in 1806. [2] Humate has also been mined in New Mexico for soil use since the 1970s. [2]

On T Nation, members in 2006 told others to 'look up' fulvic acid as an essential mineral in organic soil, and in 2002 a poster suggested mumie, whose active ingredient they believed to be fulvic acid, alongside vitamins and adaptogens for recovery. [7][8] In 2014 a member asked about a shilajit fulvic complex included in a multi-ingredient stack. [9]

Some shilajit samples contain hazardous heavy metals including lead, and a 2024 review examined heavy-metal toxicity in shilajit. [3] A 2014 review stated that shilajit safety is well documented in animal and human studies, while also saying more controlled work on standardised products is needed. [4] A 2025 review notes possible cytotoxicity under some conditions. [6]

A 2014 review reported that animal and human studies indicate shilajit enhances spermatogenesis and supports physical performance and fatigue relief, and that fulvic acid and dibenzo-alpha-pyrones appear to be key constituents. [4] A 2023 study reported fulvic acid attenuated atopic dermatitis signs through CCL17/22 downregulation (preclinical). [10]

Registered trials include one on metabolic syndrome starting November 2026 and another on epigenetic ageing markers starting May 2026, both with 60 participants and recruiting. [11][12] No trial has examined fulvic acid for appearance outcomes.
